html:
Liberation theology is a movement in Christian thought that says the church must stand with the poor and work to free them from injustice, not only from sin. It grew in the Catholic Church in Latin America in the 1960s and 1970s.

Its founding book is A Theology of Liberation (1971) by the Peruvian priest Gustavo Gutiérrez, who worked in the slums of Lima, Peru. The opening of the church after the Second Vatican Council, and a meeting of Latin American bishops at Medellín in 1968, gave it room to grow. Its key phrase was a "preferential option for the poor".

In practice it meant small "base communities" where poor Catholics read the Bible together and organised for land, schools and rights. Archbishop Óscar Romero of El Salvador, who spoke out against army killings, was shot dead while saying Mass in 1980.

Critics said it borrowed too much from Karl Marx. In the 1980s the Vatican, under Pope John Paul II, disciplined some of its thinkers, such as the Brazilian Leonardo Boff. Later Pope Francis, from Argentina, welcomed Gutiérrez and made Romero a saint.
sum: Liberation theology is a movement in Christian thought that says the church must stand with the poor and work to free them from injustice, not only from sin. It grew in the Catholic Church in Latin America in the 1960s and 1970s.
